feedback: If a learner drops 'It melted because the sun was warm' into WHAT I SAW, highlight the word 'because': 'That's a great IDEA about why — but did you SEE the sun make it melt, or are you thinking it?'
For 'the ice got smaller' in WHAT I SAW: confirm — everyone watching would agree they saw this.
If a learner calls 'the ice was sad' an observation, ask whether sadness is something you can see, or a feeling you are giving the ice.
Affirm interpretations: 'Thinking about why is useful science — we just want to label it as an idea, not call it something we saw.'
activities.intendedInsight: The puddle shrinking is something everyone would agree on; the 'because…' is a story I added, and my story might be wrong — so keeping it separate from what I saw is what lets me later test or change it.
learnerActions: Watch or recall a vivid shared event, e.g. an ice cube in a sunny window slowly turning to a puddle.
Take statement cards one at a time and place each into a WHAT I SAW bin or a WHAT I THINK bin. Examples to sort: 'The ice got smaller', 'The ice was sad', 'It melted because the sun was warm'.
When sorting 'It melted because the sun was warm', notice the word 'because' — ask yourself: did I SEE the sun make it melt, or am I thinking that?
Say aloud why each 'saw' card is something everyone looking would agree on.

Discuss how the same observation ('the puddle got smaller') could have more than one explanation (the sun dried it, or the water soaked into the ground) — both of which are ideas about why, not things seen.
activities.title: Two Buckets: sort what I saw from what I think

feedback: When only the observation remains, confirm it 'glows' as pure observation: everyone could agree on it.
If a learner leaves 'because the sun was warm' attached, point out that this is the why-idea, not something seen.
For 'the sun dried up the puddle', prompt: turn it into something you could actually observe — e.g. 'the puddle got smaller'.
activities.intendedInsight: Stripping a statement back to the observation is an active move that shows which part was the evidence and which part was my explanation added on top.
learnerActions: Take a mixed sentence such as 'The ice melted because the sun was warm' or 'The sun dried up the puddle'.
Cross out or remove the interpretation part so only what was actually observed remains (e.g. 'The ice melted' / 'The puddle got smaller').
Read the trimmed sentence back and check that everyone watching would agree it is what happened.
Then, separately, state your interpretation starting with 'I think…' so both layers are named and kept apart.
activities.title: Snip the 'because' tail: rewrite to a pure observation

feedback: Praise the child for catching their own interpretation and relabelling it.
If the child gives a cause as a 'saw' answer, ask again: 'Did you see that happen, or did you see something and guess why?'
When a child offers a second explanation, affirm that this shows the idea is separate from the fact.
An adult may need to scaffold the wording: at 6–7 many children cannot yet articulate the saw/think split unaided, so model the two sentence starters if they stall.
activities.intendedInsight: A single moment splits into two things — the seen fact and my idea about why — and one observation can support more than one 'why'.
learnerActions: Look at a shared picture or scene (melting snowman, wilting plant, rolling ball).
Answer two separate questions in turn: first 'What did you actually SEE?', then 'What do you THINK that means?'
Notice and name any time an idea slips into the 'saw' answer, and move it to the 'think' answer.
Offer a second possible explanation for the same thing you saw.
activities.title: Science-buddy dialogue: 'What did you SEE? What do you THINK it means?'

feedback: For a correctly flagged mixed statement, confirm the give-away word that signalled the hidden idea if there is one (e.g. 'because'); if there is no such word (e.g. 'The sun dried up the puddle'), confirm the part that claims a cause or feeling nobody actually saw.
For an error, return to the 'could I actually see this?' test rather than giving the answer outright.
activities.intendedInsight: I can reliably tell a seen fact from an idea about why, including in tricky mixed wording.
learnerActions: Given short vivid statements, label each as an observation or an interpretation. Include tempting mixed statements as the hard cases.
Complete sentence frames: 'I observed …' with a pure observation, and 'I think …' with the matching interpretation.
Explain for one item how you can tell which is which.
activities.title: Check: observation or interpretation?
